OTHER ASPECTS OF ASTHMA MANAGEMENT Other therapeutic approaches for the management of asth- ma are currently under investigation. Ultra-long-acting beta2 agonists under development such as carmoterol, GSK-159797 (TD-3327), and indacaterol are suitable for once daily use, leading to increased convenience for pa- tients.53 Carbamazepine has shown potential as a treat- ment for asthma in addition to regular asthma therapy;54 improved lung function and fewer exacerbations have been reported. The recombinant human B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), nesiritide, has been reported to be an effec- tive bronchodilator when given intravenously;55 its clini- cal role, if any, remains to be determined. As well as their established antibacterial effect, it has been suggested that macrolides also have immunomodulatory effects that could be useful in the management of respiratory diseases. However, a systematic review1 found insufficient evi- dence to support or refute the use of macrolides in chronic asthma although some clinical data indicated a positive ef- fect; routine use was not recommended and further studies were warranted. Ketolides also appear to have immu- nomodulatory effects: a 10-day course of oral telithromy- cin started with standard treatment for acute asthma in adults was reported to improve asthma symptoms, regard- less of infection with Chlamydophila pneumoniae (Chlamydia pneumoniae) or Mycoplasma pneumoniae.56 The mechanism of this effect is unclear, however, and fur- ther studies are needed.57 Interestingly, furosemide given by inhalation has been found to protect against bronchoconstriction induced by exercise58 and external stimuli,59,60 but was not effective in improving bronchial hyperresponsiveness in a 4-week study,61 and provided no additional benefit when added to salbutamol for the treatment of acute asthma in a small study in children.62 Any clinical application has yet to be determined.63 There has been some interest in heparin given by inhalation,63-65 and nebulised lidocaine may be of some benefit;63,66,67 intravenous lidocaine or oral mexilet- ine have been shown to block reflex bronchoconstric- tion.68 Inhaled magnesium sulfate may also be of some ad- junctive benefit to beta2 agonists in the management of acute episodes.69 There is increasing study of the cellular mechanisms of in- flammation in asthma and ways of controlling them.70 Phosphodiesterase type-4 is an enzyme that hydrolyses cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cyclic AMP), stimulat- ing the release of acute inflammatory mediators and im- Bronchodilators and Anti-asthma Drugs 1111 The symbol † de
